title: Brain-Infecting Fungus Detections Quadruple in US, CDC Report Warns
excerpt: Cladophialophora bantiana cases rose to 14 in 2025 at a national reference lab, with a 60% to 70% fatality rate, no national tracking system, and no confirmed explanation for the increase.
body:
• Detections of the brain-infecting fungus Cladophialophora bantiana nearly quadrupled between 2023 and 2025, the CDC reports, rising to 8 cases in 2024 and 14 in 2025 at a University of Washington reference laboratory.
  • From January 2009 to July 2026 the lab identified 48 confirmed cases and one probable case across 21 states and Washington, D.C.; California had 6, Florida 5, Texas 5 and Pennsylvania 4.
  • The infection forms brain abscesses and carries a 60% to 70% fatality rate even with aggressive treatment, and about half of patients had no weakened immune system.
  • There is no national tracking system; anyone with persistent severe headache, vision or memory changes after a suspected brain abscess should seek prompt specialist care — early diagnosis is difficult and treatment usually needs surgery plus multiple antifungal drugs.

A rare fungus that can infect the brain and kill up to seven in ten patients is being detected far more often in the United States, according to a new report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention summarised by Fox News and the New York Post. Public health officials are calling for heightened clinical awareness and systematic national tracking because the reasons for the increase are not yet known.

The organism, Cladophialophora bantiana, is a dark-pigmented, yeast-like mould found in soil and decaying matter around the world. It is unusual among invasive fungi because it targets the central nervous system and can cross into brain tissue, where it forms abscesses made up of pus and dead tissue.

What the CDC data show

Researchers reviewed samples handled by a microbiology laboratory at the University of Washington. Between January 2009 and July 2026 they identified 48 confirmed cases and one probable case. For most of that period the fungus was exceptionally rare, with only one to five detections a year from 2009 through 2023. Detections then rose to eight in 2024 and 14 in 2025.

https://x.com/Rainmaker1973/status/2111140062947668367

The increase was not explained simply by more testing. Measured against all central nervous system specimens submitted for fungal analysis, detections rose from an average of 8.4 per 1,000 specimens in 2017 to 2023 to 26 per 1,000 in 2025. Most samples, 88 percent, came from brain tissue and 12 percent from lung tissue, supporting the theory that inhalation is a main route of exposure, although entry through a skin wound is also presumed possible.

The median patient age was 68. Cases were geographically dispersed rather than confined to one outbreak site, a pattern that makes a single point source unlikely and points instead to wider environmental exposure or improved recognition.

Why doctors find it so hard to treat

About half of infections occurred in people who were otherwise healthy, which sets this fungus apart from many mould infections that mainly strike patients with severely weakened immune systems. Lead author Joshua Lieberman told reporters the pattern was alarming because healthy people were also at high risk of death. A short comment in the coverage captured that concern.

"We think that we're probably undersampling."

— Joshua Lieberman, lead author

Diagnosis often comes late. A brain abscess caused by the fungus can be mistaken for a tumour, and standard spinal-fluid tests may miss it. In one fatal case described in the coverage, PCR tests on spinal fluid were negative both a month before and at the time of a brain biopsy. Treatment typically requires surgery to remove infected tissue combined with several antifungal medicines, yet a systematic review cited in the report still found a fatality rate of 60 percent to 70 percent even with aggressive care.

Why cases may be rising

The CDC states plainly that the reasons for the apparent increase are unknown. Researchers have raised a possible climate link for study, not as a proven cause: the fungus has historically been associated with warmer, humid conditions, warmer temperatures may allow more fungal pathogens to survive in new environments, and a similar jump was reported in France in 2022, its warmest year on record.

What is clear is the surveillance gap. Without a federal tracking system, the University of Washington figures are likely an underestimate of the true national total, because not every hospital sends specimens to that laboratory.

What readers should do

This remains a rare infection, and the reports do not suggest person-to-person spread or a need for the general public to change daily behaviour. Clinicians are being advised to consider this fungus when a suspected brain abscess does not respond as expected, so biopsy and specialised testing happen earlier. Anyone experiencing severe persistent headache with neurological symptoms such as vision change, confusion or weakness should seek urgent medical care rather than waiting for symptoms to resolve.
